client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time I'm around family, it just feels... hollow, I guess. Like there's this huge gap where she used to be, and instead of feeling comforted by everyone around me, I just feel her absence even more. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist: Thank you for being here and for giving this a chance, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — that kind of courage matters. The way you describe that hollow feeling around family really speaks to how grief can make the people closest to us feel like a reminder of the loss rather than a comfort, and that's such a painful and disorienting experience. I'm wondering, when you think about your grandmother and that gap she's left, what do you miss most about her presence?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I miss the way she just... accepted me without needing me to explain myself. Like I didn't have to perform or be okay around her, I could just exist and that was enough. And now when I'm with my family, everyone's either falling apart or pretending everything's fine, and I don't know how to be either of those things.
therapist: What you've described — having someone who let you just *be* without performing — is such a rare and precious gift, and it makes complete sense that her absence would feel especially isolating in moments where you feel pressure to fit into one of those two roles. I notice as you're talking about this, there's a lot coming out quickly, like maybe there's more weight behind those words than even you're letting yourself sit with right now. What does it feel like in your body when you're in those family moments, caught between those two ways of being?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I mean... when I'm at those family gatherings, there's this tightness that starts in my chest pretty early on, like before I even walk through the door sometimes. It kind of spreads up into my shoulders and jaw, and I'm already bracing for which version of me I'm going to have to be. And then I feel guilty for even resenting it, because these are my people, you know, I should want to be there.
therapist: That physical bracing before you even walk through the door is your body telling you something really important — it's already anticipating the emotional labor ahead, and that's exhausting in a way that goes beyond just missing your grandmother. The guilt you feel for resenting it makes a lot of sense too, because loving people and finding them hard to be around right now aren't contradictory things — grief can make both true at the same time. I'm curious, when you imagine a version of those gatherings where you didn't have to be *any* particular way, what would that even look like for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I honestly don't even know what that would look like, because I've spent so long trying to hold everything together at those gatherings that I'm not sure I know how to just... be there without a role. Like, I'm always the one making sure everyone's okay, deflecting the awkward silences, keeping things moving — and if I stopped doing that, I think I'd just feel even more lost and guilty for not contributing. It's almost easier to stay busy than to actually sit with how much I miss her.
therapist: It sounds like staying busy and being the caretaker for everyone else has become a way of avoiding the one thing that's hardest to face — actually sitting with how much you miss her. And there's something really telling in what you just said: that stopping would make you feel *lost*, as though your sense of purpose in those rooms has quietly replaced the space where your grief lives. I wonder, who was taking care of *you* at those gatherings before she was gone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That question kind of stopped me cold, honestly. I don't think anyone was, really — she was the one who checked in on me, made sure I'd eaten, noticed if I seemed off. And now you're pointing that out and I feel this weird mix of sad and almost... embarrassed, like I should have seen that sooner.
therapist: There's nothing to be embarrassed about — it's actually really hard to see the things that feel most natural to us, and she was probably so good at caring for you that it just felt like the air in the room. What strikes me is that even as you're saying something quite painful, your voice has gone very soft and quiet, like part of you is holding this realization gently rather than letting yourself fully feel the weight of it. What would it be like to let yourself actually grieve *that* — not just losing her, but losing the one person who made sure you were okay?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I don't know if I can do that. Like, when you say "let yourself grieve it," I understand what you mean intellectually, but every time I start to go toward that feeling, something in me just... shuts it down, like a door slamming. I think part of me is scared that if I actually let myself feel how alone I am without her, it'll just confirm that there's no one else out there who will ever care about me that way again.
therapist: That fear makes so much sense — that if you open the door fully, you might find something unbearable waiting on the other side. But I want to gently reflect something back to you: the way you just said that came out very quickly, almost like the words were trying to outrun the feeling itself, which tells me that door isn't as shut as it might seem. What if the grief isn't actually confirming that you'll never be cared for that way again, but rather showing you just how deeply you *deserve* that kind of care?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know... when you say I "deserve" that kind of care, something in me wants to push back on that immediately, like there's a voice that says "well, if you deserved it, you'd still have it." It's hard to sit with the idea that the loneliness I feel now is somehow proof of something good about me rather than proof that I'm just... hard to stay close to. And yeah, maybe you're right that the door isn't fully shut, because even talking about it right now I can feel something tightening in my chest that I really don't want to look at directly.
therapist: That voice that says "if you deserved it, you'd still have it" is such a cruel and convincing kind of logic, but it's also a thought, not a fact — and it's worth noticing that it showed up *instantly*, like it's been waiting to shut down any moment of self-compassion before it can take root. The tightening in your chest right now, the thing you don't want to look at directly — I don't think that's proof that you're hard to love; I think that might actually be the grief of someone who loved and was loved very deeply. What do you think she would say if she heard you describe yourself as hard to stay close to?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know... I think she would probably push back on it, tell me I'm being too hard on myself. But that almost makes it worse, you know? Because then I just feel guilty for not being able to believe it when she said things like that, like maybe I was too caught up in my own head to really let her in the way she deserved.
therapist: The guilt you're carrying right now — that you somehow failed her by not fully receiving her love — is such a heavy thing to hold, and I want to gently challenge it: the fact that you struggled to believe her doesn't mean you didn't let her in, it means you were human, and she almost certainly knew that. It's also striking that even as you're saying something quite painful, there's a quickness in how you're moving through it, like you're already rushing toward the guilt before you let yourself feel how much it meant that she kept saying those things anyway. What if her pushing back on your self-criticism, over and over, was actually her way of staying close to you — and that *was* real, even if you couldn't fully receive it at the time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it's hard not to feel like I was just... taking from her without really giving back what she needed. Like, she kept showing up and I kept doubting her, and that feels like a failure on my part no matter how you frame it. And yeah, maybe I am rushing past the feeling of it, because if I slow down and actually sit with how much it meant that she kept trying, it just makes the loss feel even bigger and I'm not sure I can handle that right now.
therapist: What you just said — "I'm not sure I can handle that" — is actually you being really honest with yourself, and that's not weakness, that's wisdom about what you need right now. But I want to sit with something you said: that you were *taking* without giving back, because from everything you've shared today, it sounds like she saw someone worth showing up for, again and again, and that's not a transaction that failed — that's love. What do you think it would mean for you to let her have been right about you, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know... it feels almost dangerous to let myself believe that, like if I accept that she was right about me, then I have to also accept that I really lost something real, and that's... that's a lot heavier than just telling myself I wasn't worth it in the first place. It's easier to be the villain in the story, you know? If I'm the one who failed her, then at least I have some kind of control over what happened.
therapist: What you just named is one of the most profound and painful things a person can realize about themselves — that self-blame can actually feel *safer* than grief, because at least blame gives you somewhere to put the pain. The way you said that, quickly and almost matter-of-factly, makes me think this insight is landing harder than you're letting on right now. I want to stay with what you said: that accepting her love means accepting the loss was real — can you tell me more about what "that's a lot heavier" actually feels like for you in this moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
